blocking.where: versions/v32/PLAN.md 'Stall classes' (class 2 'main CPU under 20 ms ...', class 4), L1 criterion 2, 'Claim boundary' ('What L1 can show'); PHYSICAL_RUN_PLAN.md 'Holds: no process-wide hold ... whether in a step or between steps'; versions/v32/l1/evaluate_l1.py lines 72-83
blocking.finding: The process-wide-hold class cannot detect a hold inside a step, so criterion 2 does not test what the plans say it tests. Class 2 requires main CPU under 20 ms over the interval. But every in-step interval contains the physics step's own CPU, at least about 39 ms in every step over 150 ms of both diagnostic runs, so an in-step hold never reaches class 2. It falls into class 6 when the step's CPU is under half the interval: L1 still fails, but the hold is labelled 'unclassified'. It falls into class 4, 'main thread working', when the step's CPU is at least half the interval, and that passes L1. Between steps the opposite error is possible. The clock client's send gap also grows past 100 ms when its own round trip to the container times out: a 0.1 s socket timeout, then a 0.1 s reconnect wait, logged as an error row. So an interval dominated by a slow ZMQ round trip, with main CPU and runnable wait both low, is classed as a hold. In addition, an interval with main CPU under 50% and runnable wait between 20 and 100 ms (part blocked, part scheduling) lands in class 6 and fails L1, although it is neither a hold nor anything the plan means to fail. The garbage-collection hold that v32 targets is still caught by criterion 1 (any collection over 20 ms) and by class 1. So the defect concerns other holds and the wording, but it sits in the pre-registered judge and in the claim boundary ('L1 can show that no process-wide hold ... occurred').
blocking.evidence: PLAN.md's rules applied to diag_v31_clock03's three in-process in-step holds (steps of 155.4, 167.8 and 265.5 ms; main CPU 39.6, 39.0 and 42.6 ms; runnable wait about 2 ms; clock-client pauses 127, 147 and 236 ms): all three come out class 6, none class 2. The v31 B stalls come out class 3 (19 of 19), and clock04's collection stalls class 1. A scratch copy of evaluate_l1.py on synthetic records gave: a 200 ms step with 40 ms of main CPU and a 190 ms clock pause, class 6; a 300 ms step with 160 ms of main CPU and a 281 ms clock pause, class 4 (passes); a 105 ms between-step interval with 3 ms of main CPU, 2 ms of wait and a 211 ms clock pause from a client timeout, class 2 (fails); a ZMQ-type wait with the clock running, class 5; a genuine between-step hold, class 2; a B step, class 3; a 120 ms collection, class 1 plus criterion-1 failure.
blocking.required_fix: Before freezing, because the judge is pre-registered and pinned: (1) define a hold by the physics thread's off-CPU time (interval minus main CPU over 100 ms), with runnable wait under 20 ms and a clock-client pause over 100 ms that contains no clock-client error row. Alternatively use the watchdog's wake-up lateness, logged continuously. That way the rule applies both inside and between steps. (2) Evaluate class 2 before class 4, or keep intervals with such a pause out of class 4. (3) State how mixed intervals (main CPU under 50%, runnable wait 20-100 ms) are classed. (4) Re-run evaluate_l1.py on synthetic cases covering all of these (in-step hold at low and at high CPU share, between-step hold, network-timeout pause, ZMQ wait, B, collection), and record that check. (5) Align PLAN.md, PHYSICAL_RUN_PLAN.md and the claim boundary with the rule.

non_blocking.where: RESULT.md 'Answer' ('none of the 13 gaps would have exceeded 87 ms'); section 4 ('about 84 ms'); PLAN.md basis
non_blocking.finding: These counterfactuals assume constant receipt delay. The received poses at the ends of the B gaps had receipt delays of 2.6 to 49.1 ms, so fully delivered gaps could have reached about 87 + 47, roughly 135 ms (clock04's fatal gap roughly 84-105 ms). The conclusions still hold: under 150 ms, and far under the 250 ms gate.
non_blocking.suggestion: Label them as inferences and give the bound.

non_blocking.where: evaluate_l1.py criterion 1 (loop_gc = collections from the first step on)
non_blocking.finding: Automatic generation-2 collections after the loop, while the result files are written, would also count. Collection durations are wall time, so a short explicit collection preempted under host load could exceed 20 ms. The risk is low: none of about 7,900 young and middle collections in clock04 exceeded 2.6 ms.
non_blocking.suggestion: Bound the window at the last step's end, and consider recording the collecting thread's CPU time per collection.

non_blocking.finding: 'received' includes offers the bridge rejected; analyze_linux.py keeps only accepted ones.
The 'bridge timer' threshold (received at least 10 ms before the next pose) equals the timer period. Normal timer jitter can then blame the bridge timer in borderline cases.
non_blocking.suggestion: Use a margin (for example 15-20 ms), or report the distribution of receive gaps for superseded poses.
